title: Which Feedback Works for Whom? Differential Effects of LLM-Generated Feedback Elements Across Learner Profiles
extended_summary:
This paper examines how specific design elements of LLM-generated feedback affect student learning and feedback acceptance, and whether those effects differ across learner personality profiles. Rather than comparing AI feedback against teacher feedback or other non-AI supports, the study asks which feedback elements within AI-generated feedback are most useful for helping students revise incorrect answers and which are rated most positively by students. The authors focus on six feedback elements derived from prior work: Baseline, Keywords, Actionability, Novelty, Coverage, and Positivity.

The intervention consisted of GPT-5-generated feedback for multiple-choice high school biology questions. Students answered questions in a web-based system, received immediate feedback tailored to the selected answer option, rated the feedback on six subjective criteria, and, if initially incorrect, revised their answers repeatedly until correct. The feedback was generated in advance and varied by element, such as emphasizing keywords, providing actionable revision guidance, increasing informational coverage, or using positive tone. The study also collected Big Five personality questionnaire data and clustered learners to examine whether feedback preferences varied by personality profile.

Participants were 321 first-year high school students in nine basic biology classes in Japan. The activity was assigned as winter-break homework, so the implementation appears to have been outside regular class time via an online system. The task context was biology problem solving rather than writing, revision of essays, or literacy instruction. Outcomes included two behavioral learning measures related to answer revision and six self-reported feedback evaluation measures including trustworthiness, review guidance, ease of understanding, key-points clarity, expression quality, and new knowledge.

The main conclusions are that Baseline, Coverage, and Keywords were the strongest feedback elements for supporting movement toward correct answers during revision, while Keywords, Baseline, and Actionability tended to receive the highest subjective ratings. Personality-based learner clusters showed different feedback preferences, suggesting potential value in personalizing AI-generated feedback. However, this is not a head-to-head comparator study against teacher feedback, peer review, automated writing evaluation, or other non-generative supports, and it does not address K-12 writing outcomes. Its evidence is therefore more relevant to AI feedback design in science learning than to claims about generative AI as a writing intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a sizable empirical K-12 experiment with direct student outcomes and structured comparisons across feedback conditions, but it is not a head-to-head generative-AI-versus-human comparator study and does not clearly report randomization details, standardized effect sizes, or strong causal controls typical of top-tier RCT evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but uneven benefits for specific feedback designs on immediate answer revision and subjective acceptance, with unclear magnitude because standardized effect estimates are not reported. Effects are short-term, task-specific, and not tied to broader writing or externally measured achievement gains.

interventions.use_case: GPT-5-generated automated feedback on high-school biology multiple-choice responses, varying six feedback design elements (baseline, keywords, actionability, novelty, coverage, positivity) to support answer revision and examine learner perceptions by personality profile.
Use of a modern large language model (GPT-5) to generate personalized-style explanatory feedback for students' incorrect answers in a web-based homework system.

finding.finding_summary: In a learning experiment with 321 first-year Japanese high school students, LLM-generated feedback supported revision on biology multiple-choice items, but effectiveness varied by feedback element. Among students initially incorrect, first revised-attempt accuracy was highest for Baseline (65.66%, n=198), followed by Coverage (53.22%, n=171) and Keywords (52.94%, n=204), while Positivity was lowest (46.63%, n=208); no standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals beyond plotted 95% CIs were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy of first revised attempt after feedback on biology multiple-choice questions; authors also report an 'Effectiveness' metric based on number of attempts to reach the correct answer.
finding.study_size: n=321 overall; per-condition initially incorrect subsamples: Baseline n=198, Keywords n=204, Actionability n=202, Novelty n=213, Coverage n=171, Positivity n=208
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported graphically only; exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Students' subjective evaluations of LLM-generated feedback differed by design element and by personality cluster. Keywords ranked first on 4 of 6 evaluation criteria and Baseline and Actionability were also consistently highly rated, whereas Positivity received relatively low ratings; Kruskal-Wallis tests showed significant cluster differences across all six criteria (p < .05), with Dunn post-hoc tests indicating Cluster 1 differed from other clusters on Trustworthiness, New Knowledge, and Expression Quality (reported p < .01 for Trustworthiness pairwise comparisons).
finding.measure: Three-point student ratings of trustworthiness, review guidance, expression quality, ease of understanding, key-points clarity, and new knowledge; personality-cluster differences in acceptance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined feedback features intended to support revision and metacognitive processing, finding that Actionability was subjectively valued but did not outperform Baseline or Coverage on revision accuracy. Authors interpret effective feedback as that which clearly directs attention to task-relevant information and provides sufficient guidance for revision, but no direct metacognition effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Revision-oriented feedback usefulness, especially 'Review Guideline' ratings and answer-revision performance.
